Sureon: A Benchmark and Vision-Language Model for Surgical Reasoning

Alejandra Perez Affiliation: Intuitive Surgical Inc., USA Email: alejandra.perezrondon@intusurg.comhttps://aperezr20.github.io/sureon    Anita Rau Affiliation: Intuitive Surgical Inc., USA Email: anita.rau@intusurg.comhttps://aperezr20.github.io/sureon    Busisiwe Mlambo Affiliation: Intuitive Surgical Inc., USA    Lee White Affiliation: Intuitive Surgical Inc., USA    Aina Brunet Affiliation: Hospital Universitari Bellvitge, Spain    Juan Verde Affiliation: IHU Strasbourg, France Affiliation: University of Strasbourg, CNRS, France    Juan Caicedo Affiliation: Fundación Santa Fe de Bogotá, Colombia    Joël L. Lavanchy Affiliation: University Digestive Health Care Center – Clarunis, Switzerland Affiliation: University of Basel, Switzerland    Adam Schmidt Affiliation: Intuitive Surgical Inc., USA    Chinedu Nwoye Affiliation: Intuitive Surgical Inc., USA    Omid Mohareri Affiliation: Intuitive Surgical Inc., USA    Muhammad Abdullah Jamal Affiliation: Intuitive Surgical Inc., USA
Abstract

A capable surgical AI model should reason from visual evidence; yet, many existing surgical benchmarks can be partially solved without visual input, as models may exploit procedural priors or common anatomy–instrument interactions to infer answers from language alone. To address this, we introduce Sureon, a video question-answering (QA) dataset and benchmark designed to evaluate visually grounded surgical reasoning. Our pipeline generates QA pairs from narrated surgical academic videos, refines incorrect options using multiple models to reduce linguistic biases, and uses trained adversarial guessers to filter out questions answerable without visual evidence. The resulting dataset contains 76K training pairs covering 168 procedures and 10 specialties, alongside a benchmark of 340 questions across 10 categories verified by expert surgeons. Benchmarking leading commercial and open-source models shows that surgical visual reasoning remains largely unsolved—no model exceeds 53% accuracy and even expert surgeons reach only 64.9%. We also introduce Sureon-VLM, a baseline trained on our curated data that avoids language shortcuts, outperforms existing open-source models on Sureon, and matches larger specialist models on multiple standard surgical benchmarks. Our training ablations show that distractor refinement and blind curation strengthen visual grounding, increasing the multimodal gain from 8.7 to 29.1 percentage points while reducing the training set from 176.6K to 76K filtered samples. Sureon thus offers both a verified testbed for surgical visual reasoning and training data that strengthens visual grounding.

1 Introduction

Surgeons perceive complex visual cues in the operative scene and constantly interpret their clinical meaning, such as whether a dissection plane is safe or what the current tissue state implies for the next step. As AI systems are increasingly explored towards intraoperative decision support and surgical autonomy [47, 6, 53], a growing body of work has turned from traditional perception models to Vision Language Models (VLMs) to capture expert-like surgical understanding and reasoning [76, 46, 61]. Yet existing benchmarks fall short of evaluating the visually grounded reasoning that defines surgical expertise, restricting progress on models with such capabilities.

In the general domain, and increasingly in diagnostic medical fields, evaluation of VLMs has progressed from classification, recognition, and localization tasks to compositional and causal reasoning problems on visual inputs [68, 69, 17, 10, 78]. But unlike radiology and pathology, where image–report pairs already exist [28, 16], surgical video is recorded ad hoc without paired reports. The field has therefore leaned on rigid expert taxonomies, and the benchmarks built on them inherit those closed label spaces [46, 50, 34, 18, 76, 56]. Moving beyond closed label spaces requires supervision that captures how surgeons describe visual evidence, uncertainty, and clinical implications in natural language, which is hard to obtain at scale.

A particularly rich and scalable source of supervision for surgical VLMs is expert-narrated video lectures that are available for training and communication of best practices. Previous work converts these lectures into open-ended instruction data to train generative surgical assistants [31, 32, 60]. Such pipelines scale up data generation by leveraging state-of-the-art (SOTA) Large Language Models (LLMs), but they provide limited verification that benchmark questions indeed require visual evidence. It remains unclear whether a high score reflects visual reasoning or just memorized surgical facts—a shortcut recent studies have documented in surgery [54] and beyond [4]. Video lectures are the rare setting in which visual cues and their clinical meaning are made explicit in language; a benchmark built from them should thus evaluate visual reasoning grounded in the surgical scene, not medical knowledge.

The challenge, therefore, is not to generate surgical QA pairs at scale, but to verify that answering them requires vision. Standard multimodal benchmark construction delegates this task to state-of-the-art LLMs: they generate questions, answers, and distractors, judge sample quality, and grade the responses of competing models [63, 33, 35]. In surgery, every link of this chain is circular. Existing multimodal models perform poorly on visual surgical tasks, and a model cannot grade an exam it would fail itself. The fallback, routing every sample through surgeons, does not scale: expert annotation is the field’s long-standing bottleneck. But skipping verification has a cost: in the general domain, large fractions of popular multimodal benchmarks have been shown to be solvable by text-only models, defeating the purpose of multimodal evaluation [15].

Rather than entrusting one general-domain model to generate, judge, and grade its own exam in a domain where it performs poorly, we propose a multi-stage agentic pipeline that yields Sureon, a video QA dataset for surgical visual reasoning. Our data generation pipeline first identifies Semantic Grounding Moments (SGMs), time intervals where the surgeon explicitly ties a semantic cue to the visual scene, and converts them into QA pairs spanning ten question types including local action reasoning, forecasting, and safety. Second, retrieval-augmented, multi-model distractor refinement aligns generated distractors with the style of correct answers to minimize statistical biases and mixes LLM generators from different families to remove single-model artifacts. Third, a blind-testing protocol discards samples that an ensemble of finetuned and off-the-shelf LLM & VLM guessers answers consistently without the video, and an iterative hardening search applies further adversarial pressure to surviving test samples. Lastly, a team of six surgeons verify a subset of the final dataset.

We introduce Sureon, a resource that consists of over 70K rigorously curated video QA pairs for training (Sureon-DB) and 340 expert-reviewed samples for benchmarking. Extensive benchmarking shows that leading commercial and open-source models struggle to reason about visual cues in surgical videos. We further show that a model trained on Sureon-DB yields higher multimodal accuracy gains with fewer training samples than naively generated surgical QA data as it is less reliant on language shortcuts. This model substantially outperforms existing open-source models, and is competitive with leading commercial systems.

2 Related Work

Surgical vision–language benchmarks. Surgical benchmarks for multi-modal understanding were first built by translating the annotations of existing datasets into language, reformulating phase, action, and tool labels into VQA pairs [49, 71, 61, 22]. Since these benchmarks were confined to a single procedure, other efforts have aggregated annotations from multiple annotated sources into cross-procedure benchmarks such as SurgVLM-Bench [76], EndoBench [34], and SurgMLLMBench [18] to assess generalization across interventions and tasks. While such annotations give a broad, systematic representation of a scene’s observable semantics, these benchmarks stay bound to the rigid label sets of their sources, never reaching perception or reasoning beyond their fixed taxonomies. To mitigate these limitations, recent work has leveraged narrated surgical procedures to source supervision from expert lectures: SurgCoT [60] uses narration to probe reasoning such as causal action ordering and cue–action alignment, though its open-ended QA format restricts systematic scoring, while SurgPub-Video [32] structures narration-derived questions as multiple choice for unambiguous evaluation. However, none of these approaches filter out questions answerable from language priors alone—as is now standard in vision-language benchmark construction in other domains [10, 67, 66, 14]—nor do they evaluate models when no visual input is provided, despite evidence that Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) score deceptively high on visual perception benchmarks under blind testing [4, 54, 44]. Concurrent work SurgCheck [54] diagnoses this shortcut reliance via paired questions that replace entity names in the question with spatial grounding cues, but is a post-hoc diagnostic tool that requires scene-graph annotations and stays constrained within existing perception ontologies. Sureon instead addresses shortcut reliance at construction time by curating questions under blind-test conditions to encourage visual reliance during both training and evaluation and targeting visual reasoning capabilities beyond fixed label spaces.

Multimodal models in surgery. Data scarcity first made CLIP-style dual-encoder models predominant in surgery, pretrained on lecture narration through contrastive alignment and extended with hierarchical objectives and LLM-based text denoising [73, 72, 42]. Although these models can match a scene to a label, they cannot describe, explain, or reason. Generative surgical MLLMs followed to cover these needs, some trained on instruction data derived from the classification and spatial annotations of existing datasets [50, 76] and others on narration-sourced supervision [62, 32], with recent work targeting reasoning rather than perception alone [56]. Concurrently, annotation- and narration-derived supervision have been integrated into a single training corpus with better generalization [9].

Automated VQA generation. Since manual annotation does not scale, recent benchmarks synthesize VQA pairs automatically from annotations or narrations with LLMs, typically in multiple-choice form for objective scoring [77]. However, naively generated options introduce language shortcuts: distractors leave statistical artifacts in length, specificity, or style that models exploit without visual grounding [65], and many questions stay answerable from textual priors alone, allowing that blind LLMs achieve high performance [15]. Two remedies have emerged to suppress this leakage: refining questions through chain-of-thought rewriting or length-matched distractors [10, 67], and removing text-answerable items via blind testing that discards any question a text-only LLM answers consistently across trials [74, 66, 52]. Such curation is often drastic: ExAct [67] retains only ∼0.9%{\sim}0.9\% of its pool, for instance. These pipelines, however, rely almost exclusively on off-the-shelf LLMs prompted zero-shot, which underestimate exploitable leakage; a text-only model fine-tuned on the answer distribution can still solve items that such zero-shot testers pass [4]. This fine-tuned-guesser signal has so far been used primarily to audit completed benchmarks rather than to curate samples during generation. In contrast, Sureon integrates distractor refinement, blind filtering, and fine-tuned guesser feedback into a single construction pipeline for surgical video QA.

3 SUREON Dataset, Benchmark, and Model

Moving beyond the closed-space recognition of predefined taxonomies, Sureon tests whether VLMs can reason over actions, states, safety-relevant events, and procedural progression in surgical video. Built from a heterogeneous pool of narrated minimally-invasive laparoscopic and robot-assisted procedures across multiple specialties, it comprises two complementary resources: Sureon-DB, a large and diverse training database of 76,061 automatically pseudo-labeled Video QA pairs for adapting VLMs to surgery, spanning 10 specialties and 168 procedure types, and Sureon, a 340-sample, surgeon-verified benchmark for rigorous assessment. This benchmark is highly diverse (8 specialties and 69 procedure types; fewer than DB as the benchmark is drawn from the smaller expert-verified validation split) and comparable in size with widely used benchmarks in other domains [20, 75, 70]. Unlike previous work (see Table 1), this data allows not only training surgical VLMs but also systematically assessing their visual reasoning capabilities. For more details, key attributes are summarized in Table 2.

Sureon unifies a broad set of capabilities within a single evaluation framework, organized into 10 categories across two temporal granularities (Figure 2). In short temporal windows, it evaluates recognition of anatomical structures, instruments, instrument-action interactions, entity states, and safety-driven actions, together with locally grounded action reasoning. In longer contexts, Sureon evaluates procedural reasoning through sequence summarization, temporal ordering, and prediction of the next procedural step. The first eight categories are posed as single-answer multiple-choice questions, while sequence summarization and temporal ordering are open-ended.

3.1 Dataset Construction

As illustrated in Figure 3, we introduce a four-stage automated pipeline to build Sureon. The pipeline addresses three challenges in surgical video-language dataset construction: (i) narrations are selective and do not densely describe all visible content, (ii) naively LLM generated multiple-choice distractors introduce linguistic shortcuts that can be exploited by other LLMs to successfully guess the correct answer, and (iii) some generated questions may be answerable from prior procedural knowledge without requiring visual evidence. To mitigate these, we first identify Semantic Grounding Moments (SGMs) from narration transcripts and use them as anchors for QA generation, then we systematically refine multiple-choice distractors to mitigate linguistic biases, and finally curate the dataset by removing questions that are solvable without accessing the video, followed by expert verification to consolidate the benchmark.

Stage 1: Raw transcript-grounded QA synthesis

In lectures, surgeons describe predominantly clinically salient events, transitions, and safety-relevant observations, so transcripts alone do not offer dense visual supervision for VLM learning. We therefore anchor QA synthesis to Semantic Grounding Moments (SGMs) in the narration (examples in Figure 6 in the Appendix B.2.2).

Given a video viv_{i} and its aligned transcript of timestamped narrated sentences (formalized in Appendix B.2), each SGM, zi​jkz_{ij}^{k} is a temporal window in which the narration provides task-specific supervision for a visually observable surgical concept:

zi​jk=(vi​[ts,te],si​j,ck),z_{ij}^{k}=\left(v_{i}[t_{s},t_{e}],\;s_{ij},\;c_{k}\right), (1)

where vi​[ts,te]v_{i}[t_{s},t_{e}] is the video clip, si​js_{ij} is the supporting transcript context, ckc_{k} is the target semantic category, and i,j,ki,j,k index video, clip, and category.

To extract SGMs at scale and convert them into QA samples, we design a pipeline of KK generator–validator agent pairs, one per semantic category in Figure 2. This decomposition follows the “divide and conquer” principle of agentic data synthesis [38, 21], in which role and category specialization yields higher data quality than prompting a single LLM. Formally, the generation–validation pipeline is described as follows:

  • •

    Generation: Given a transcript TiT_{i}, generator 𝒜k\mathcal{A}_{k} identifies the intervals in which the surgeon explicitly describes content relevant to its assigned category and produces a set of instructional samples {xi​jk}j\{x_{ij}^{k}\}_{j}, each defined as:

    xi​jk=(vi​[ts,te],Qi​jk,Ai​jk,𝒪i​jk),x_{ij}^{k}=\left(v_{i}[t_{s},t_{e}],\;Q_{ij}^{k},\;A_{ij}^{k},\;\mathcal{O}_{ij}^{k}\right), (2)

    where Qi​jkQ_{ij}^{k} is the question, Ai​jkA_{ij}^{k} the answer, and 𝒪i​jk\mathcal{O}_{ij}^{k} the set of multiple-choice options, when applicable.

  • •

    Validation: The paired validator filters the generator’s output by enforcing category-specific constraints alongside four universal criteria: hallucination filtering, visual grounding, temporal-window correctness, and semantic deduplication (detailed in Appendix B.2.3). The output of Stage 1 is a transcript-grounded set of surgical video QA pairs 𝒟SGM={xi​jk}i,j,k\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{SGM}}=\{x_{ij}^{k}\}_{i,j,k}.

Additional implementation details, agent system prompts, per-category agent specifications (Table 7), and the full per-category sample breakdown (Table 6) are provided in Appendix B.2.

Stage 2: Multi-Model Retrieval-Augmented Distractor Generation for Bias Mitigation

The naively generated distractors from Stage 1 introduce two compounding biases that let models guess correctly without video. A distributional gap, where correct answers and distractors differ in length, specificity, clinical detail, and phrasing, reveals which option looks correct without any visual grounding; and model-specific artifacts—distractors from a single LLM share syntactic and lexical patterns—provide a further shortcut that becomes especially exploitable during fine-tuning. We mitigate both with a two-component strategy: (i) Retrieval-Augmented Distractor Generation (RADG) to align the distractor distribution with that of correct answers, and (ii) multi-model mixing to suppress model-specific artifacts:

(i) RADG. To close the distributional gap between correct answers and distractors, we aggregate all correct answers from the training set into a typed retrieval pool for each question category, cc:

𝒫c={Ai​jk|ck=c},\mathcal{P}_{c}=\left\{A_{ij}^{k}\;\middle|\;c_{k}=c\right\}, (3)

and encode each answer with a dense embedding model for retrieval. For each question Qi​jkQ_{ij}^{k}, we retrieve answer-style exemplars from 𝒫ck\mathcal{P}_{c_{k}}, using video metadata to favor answers from procedures similar to the current one while preserving category-wide diversity, and merge them into a unified exemplar set Ei​jkE_{ij}^{k} (Appendix B.3.1). Each generator MℓM_{\ell}, instantiated as a state-of-the-art LLM, is then conditioned on the question, its correct answer, the local transcript context, and the exemplar set Ei​jkE_{ij}^{k} to produce distractors that are factually incorrect for the transcript context, clinically plausible, and stylistically aligned with the retrieved exemplars.

(ii) Multi-model mixing. Each of the three distractor-generator LLMs (M1M_{1}, M2M_{2}, M3M_{3}) produces NN distractors, and the final set is drawn at random from the combined 3​N3N-candidate pool 𝒟i​jk,pool\mathcal{D}_{ij}^{k,\mathrm{pool}}, which empirically reduces short-cut learning compared to employing distractors from a single model (ablation in Sec. B.3). The output of Stage 2 is the refined dataset 𝒟ref\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{ref}}, in which each Stage-1 sample is paired with its refined distractor set 𝒪i​jk,ref\mathcal{O}_{ij}^{k,\mathrm{ref}}.

Stage 3: Visual-Dependence Curation via Blind-Testing Filtering

Distractor refinement reduces linguistic artifacts in the answer options, yet some samples remain answerable without the video—either from residual language shortcuts, or because LLMs can resolve certain questions from procedural knowledge acquired during pretraining. The goal of Step 3 is to remove these samples. To this end, we employ a blind-testing curation protocol: an ensemble of LLM guessers 𝒢\mathcal{G} is queried without video access, receiving only the question Qi​jkQ_{ij}^{k} and the refined options 𝒪i​jk,ref\mathcal{O}_{ij}^{k,\mathrm{ref}}. Any sample the guessers can solve is discarded. To separate genuine shortcut exploitation from lucky guesses, we query each guesser multiple times at non-zero temperature and score it by its consistency, the fraction of trials in which it recovers the correct answer, rather than by a single correct response, inspired by prior work [66, 52] (formalized in Appendix B.4.2).

To detect candidates answerable from prior knowledge alone, and to additionally account for language shortcuts that only become exploitable once a model is fine-tuned on the answer distribution, our guesser ensemble combines off-the-shelf and blind-fine-tuned models (full specification in Appendix B.4.2). We curate the training set for these fine-tuned guessers via stratified 4-fold cross-validation—guessers trained on the complementary folds and scored on the held-out fold—yielding the curated training set Sureon-DB. The validation split is evaluated by the guessers trained on the full training split and evaluated blindly, yielding 𝒟val\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{val}}.

As a final curation step for 𝒟val\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{val}}, we employ distractor hardening via iterative blind testing. We fine-tune a stronger blind guesser on Sureon-DB and, for each retained sample, iteratively resample distractor configurations from the pool 𝒟i​jk,pool\mathcal{D}_{ij}^{k,\mathrm{pool}}—subject to the cross-model diversity constraint—until the guesser fails to recover the correct answer under blind testing. The retained configuration yields the hardened validation set 𝒟val⋆\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{val}}^{\star}; samples for which no such configuration exists are discarded (Appendix B.4.3, Alg. 1).

Stage 4: Expert Verification

Samples from the hardened validation set 𝒟val⋆\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{val}}^{\star} undergo manual verification by 6 expert surgeons. Each reviewer is presented with the video clip, the aligned transcript segment, the question, the correct answer, and all distractors, and accepts a sample only when its temporal alignment, answer correctness, visual grounding, and distractor validity all hold simultaneously (Appendix B.5.2). Any sample that is rejected or flagged is discarded under a conservative retention policy, ensuring the final Sureon benchmark ℬSureon⊂𝒟val⋆\mathcal{B}_{\text{{Sureon}}}\subset\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{val}}^{\star} satisfies both visual-dependence criteria and expert clinical judgment. A dual-reviewed subset is additionally used to assess inter-rater reliability (Appendix B.5.2).

3.2 Sureon-VLM

Beyond evaluation, Sureon-DB provides a large training dataset. To assess its value, we train a surgical VLM and use it to probe two questions. First, does the standard surgical-VLM recipe generalize to reasoning? Existing surgical assistants are trained by transforming classification-annotated surgery datasets into templated instructions augmented with LLMs [76, 62]; this supervision is mostly perceptual (presence, localization, phase), leaving open whether it extends to reasoning. And second, does consolidating public templated data with Sureon yield a single model strong at both perception and reasoning?

To answer these questions, we assemble a unified instruction-tuning corpus from two complementary sources: (i) image-level annotations from public datasets (tool and anatomy localization, localized action recognition, and presence/state labels derived from them); and (ii) video clips from workflow annotations (phase, step, and action recognition). Following common practice, each annotation is mapped to a schema, rendered into natural-language QA via task-specific templates, and augmented with an LLM for linguistic diversity (Appendix C). This yields 𝒟pub\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{pub}} (5.5M QA pairs over 22 public datasets), which we combine with the Sureon training split into 𝒟all=𝒟Sureon-DB∪𝒟pub\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{all}}=\mathcal{D}_{\text{{Sureon}-DB}}\cup\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{pub}}.

We then fine-tune Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct [8] on 𝒟all\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{all}} using 8 frames per clip to obtain Sureon-VLM. We study data composition and staging order (single-stage vs. two-stage schedules) and select the best configuration; the full ablation is reported in Appendix Table 19.

4 Experiments

Experiments on the Sureon benchmark show that (i) no existing model can reliably answer complex questions about surgery, (ii) Sureon measures visual reasoning, not short-cut learning, and (iii) training on Sureon-DB does not lead to overfitting to a specific task, but we show that Sureon-VLM outperforms existing open-source VLMs on Sureon and has strong performance on traditional classification tasks in surgery.

We benchmark commercial general-purpose VLMs (GPT-5.1 [55] (high reasoning), Gemini 3.1 Pro [23] (high reasoning)); open generalist models (Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct and Qwen3-VL-32B-Thinking [8], Gemma 4 [24], Molmo2 [19]); and open medical VLMs (MedGemma 1.5 [51], MedGRPO), and include a human expert baseline. We also evaluate Sureon-VLM, our model fine-tuned on 𝒟all\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{all}}, along with the same model trained on Sureon-DB alone or the public surgical corpus alone.

Of the ten Sureon question types, eight are multiple-choice and scored by accuracy. Temporal ordering (TO) is scored by exact-match accuracy, while sequence summarization (SM) is open-ended and scored by a validated LLM judge (Appendix D). We report the mean over the accuracy-based types and report SM separately. Additionally, we report multimodal gain [15] as a complementary metric assessing how much a model’s answers reflect the surgical video rather than language priors. It is defined as the accuracy difference between a model given the visual input (SvS_{v}) and the same model answering blind (Sw​vS_{wv}): MG=Sv−Sw​v\mathrm{MG}=S_{v}-S_{wv}. We provide additional evaluation and inference details in Appendix (D.1).

Visual reasoning in surgery is an unsolved task.

Table 3 reports per-category accuracy with 95% confidence intervals on the average. Gemini 3.1 Pro obtains the highest numerical mean (μ=52.2\mu=52.2), followed by Sureon-VLM (μ=48.2\mu=48.2) and GPT-5.1 (μ=46.8\mu=46.8). However, the differences among the strongest models are not statistically significant (Appendix D.1). In contrast, the human expert baseline reaches (μ=64.9\mu=64.9) and significantly outperforms every evaluated model, indicating remaining headroom for surgical visual understanding. Expert performance also varies by category: surgeons approach ceiling on Procedure-Agnostic Action Description (96.5%), but perform substantially lower on Entity Existence (51.3%) and Local Action Reasoning (35.1%), likely reflecting specialty-specific anatomical knowledge and the added difficulty of inferring the purpose of an observed action. Models show a different pattern, with Forecasting among the hardest categories, suggesting that anticipating procedural progression remains harder than describing the current scene. Given the wider confidence intervals at the category level, we interpret these differences as broad trends rather than fine-grained rankings.

Sureon measures visual reasoning. Across the strongest models, multimodal gain remains substantial: +29.1 for Sureon-VLM, +20.4 for Gemini 3.1 Pro, and +21.1 for GPT-5.1. Notably, Sureon-VLM achieves the largest MG, indicating that its benchmark performance depends strongly on the surgical video rather than on language priors. This visual dependence is progressively strengthened by the Sureon construction pipeline. Table 4 shows that MG increases from 8.7 with the raw Stage-1 data to 16.8 after retrieval-augmented distractor generation and to 29.1 after blind-test curation. The final improvement occurs while reducing the training set from 176.6K to 76K samples. Thus, stronger visual grounding results from removing supervision that rewards language shortcuts rather than simply increasing training-set size.

Sureon-VLM has broad capabilities. The surgical field’s data scarcity has pushed existing surgical VLMs toward classification-derived datasets. The data-composition ablations in Table 3 show that training on public surgical datasets alone performs poorly on Sureon (μ=20.7\mu=20.7, MG =8.7=8.7), whereas training on Sureon-DB alone reaches μ=44.1\mu=44.1 with MG =22.1=22.1. Both Sureon-only and combined training significantly outperform public-only training after multiple-comparison correction. When combining the two sources, performance raises Sureon from 44.1 to 48.2.

Public data nevertheless remains complementary. The full Sureon-VLM is trained on both sources so that reasoning-oriented supervision from Sureon-DB is combined with conventional surgical perception supervision. Table 5 shows that this produces a model that remains competitive on established surgical perception benchmarks while also performing strongly on Sureon. Despite its 8B backbone, Sureon-VLM matches or exceeds several larger specialist models on Cholec80 and Endoscapes-CVS, while clip-level inference further improves temporal recognition. The lower performance on HeiChole action recognition suggests that breadth still comes with trade-offs relative to models optimized for narrower tasks. Consolidating reasoning and perception supervision thus yields a single model that keeps the perception abilities of specialist systems while gaining the visual reasoning they lack (Table 3).

5 Conclusions

In this work, we introduce Sureon, a high-quality surgical visual reasoning benchmark that leverages expert narration in educational videos. Rather than naively generating VQA samples from lecture videos, which can introduce language-only shortcuts, Sureon combines distractor refinement, blind-test curation, and expert review to preserve questions that require visual evidence from the surgical video. As a result, Sureon supports the training and evaluation of models across multiple semantic categories spanning perception and reasoning tasks in surgery. Our experiments show two things. First, surgical visual reasoning remains far from solved: no model exceeds 53%53\% accuracy, and multimodal gain does not exceed 29.1%29.1\%. Second, verification matters beyond data volume: removing text-solvable samples raises multimodal gain from 8.78.7 to 29.129.1 while reducing the training set size by 57.0%57.0\%. A model trained on this data matches larger specialist models on perception benchmarks while also demonstrating strong visual reasoning on Sureon, outperforming existing open-source models. Together, these findings show that progress in surgical vision–language models requires evaluating and training for dependence on visual evidence. Sureon is a step towards more reliable and visually grounded surgical reasoning.
