Supplementary Material

This supplementary material provides additional details, results, and discussion supporting the main paper. Appendix A covers limitations and future work; the remaining sections expand on the main paper: Appendix B details the four-stage construction pipeline, including the final dataset configuration (main Sec. 3.1); Appendix C details the public-data training corpus 𝒟pub\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{pub}} (main Sec. 3.2); Appendix D specifies inference and scoring protocols (main Sec. 4); Appendix E reports the training data-composition and staging ablations (main Sec. 4); and Appendix F discusses ethical considerations.

Appendix A Limitations and future work

While Sureon advances visually grounded surgical reasoning evaluation, several limitations and avenues for future work remain:

  • •

    Our refinement and blind-test curation (Sec. B.3–B.4) reduce text-solvability by operating on the answer options. However, text-solvability is partly a property of how a question is framed: a question that names the operative context or telegraphs the procedural phase can leak its answer regardless of the distractors. Jointly reframing questions alongside distractors is a natural extension that could reduce the number of removed samples in Stage 3.

  • •

    Our guesser ensemble is built from an open-source model (Qwen3-VL-8B), used off-the-shelf and in fine-tuned variants, rather than from commercial models. However, unlike previous work that only use models off-the-shelf, the fine-tuned guessers reveal language shortcuts that only become learnable once a model is exposed to the answer distribution – leakage that zero-shot off-the-shelf testers, including commercial ones, systematically underestimate [4]. Additionally, the precise set of samples removed during curation may vary under a different guesser family or as foundation models become more capable. We therefore complement overall benchmark accuracy with evaluation-time multimodal gain, M​G=Sv−Sw​vMG=S_{v}-S_{wv}, which evaluates each model both with and without visual input and measures how much of its performance is attributable to the surgical video rather than language priors or shortcuts. This provides a model-specific check for visual dependence beyond the fixed curation ensemble and allows the benchmark to remain auditable as model capabilities improve.

  • •

    Every QA pair is anchored to a Semantic Grounding Moment, excluding visually salient content that lecturers do not verbalize. Thus, our benchmark under-samples reasoning that is observable but un-narrated, and its coverage is shaped by what surgeons choose to teach rather than by everything a model could be asked to see.

  • •

    Because Sureon is sourced from educational lecture videos, the case mix likely over-represents textbook presentations, well-rehearsed techniques, and controlled operative conditions relative to the full diversity of real-world practice. Atypical anatomies, intraoperative complications, and less common surgical approaches may therefore be underrepresented, and strong benchmark performance should not be assumed to transfer to the long tail of clinical variability.

  • •

    Sureon is built from edited, narrated, minimally-invasive lecture recordings. Intraoperative video differs (uncut, without narration, with degraded visibility from smoke, blood, and motion) so strong Sureon performance does not by itself establish readiness for live surgical settings. Sureon-DB is additionally pseudo-labeled and not expert-verified; both resources are intended for research and evaluation, and not for clinical use.

Appendix B Sureon Construction Details

B.1 Data Source

Sureon is built on the SurgLaVi-β\mathbf{\beta} dataset [42], which provides timestamped transcriptions of surgical academic lectures for 3,148 YouTube videos, along with metadata on the surgical specialty, subject, and procedure type of each video.

Dataset splits. SurgLaVi-β\mathbf{\beta} was originally released as a pre-training corpus and therefore does not include predefined train/validation/test splits. We performed stratified video-level splitting based on procedure subject, ensuring that the training and validation distributions are balanced across subjects. Approximately 10% of videos were held out for validation, yielding 2,809 videos for training and 339 for validation. The resulting subject distributions are shown in Figure 5.

B.2 Stage 1: Raw transcript-grounded QA synthesis

B.2.1 Notation

Each video viv_{i} is paired with an aligned transcript Ti={(si​j,[ti​jstart,ti​jend])}j=1miT_{i}=\{(s_{ij},[t_{ij}^{\mathrm{start}},t_{ij}^{\mathrm{end}}])\}_{j=1}^{m_{i}} of mim_{i} timestamped narrated sentences, where si​js_{ij} is the jj-th narrated sentence and [ti​jstart,ti​jend][t_{ij}^{\mathrm{start}},t_{ij}^{\mathrm{end}}] its spoken interval. From this transcript, a Semantic Grounding Moment is the tuple zi​jk=(vi[ts,te],si​j:j+r,ck)z_{ij}^{k}=(v_{i}[t_{s},t_{e}],\,s_{ij:j+r},\,c_{k}), pairing a video clip vi​[ts,te]v_{i}[t_{s},t_{e}] with its supporting transcript context si​j:j+rs_{ij:j+r} and a target semantic category ckc_{k}. Each SGM is converted into one or more QA samples xi​jk=(vi​[ts,te],Qi​jk,Ai​jk,𝒪i​jk)x_{ij}^{k}=(v_{i}[t_{s},t_{e}],\,Q_{ij}^{k},\,A_{ij}^{k},\,\mathcal{O}_{ij}^{k}), where Qi​jkQ_{ij}^{k} is the question, Ai​jkA_{ij}^{k} the ground-truth answer, and 𝒪i​jk\mathcal{O}_{ij}^{k} the multiple-choice option set when applicable. This notation is used throughout the remaining construction stages.

B.2.2 Semantic Grounding Moments

Surgical narrations are sparse: even when instruments, anatomical structures, or actions are visible in the operative field, surgeons do not continuously annotate them in speech. If raw narration segments are used directly as scene descriptions, the resulting labels are incomplete and potentially misleading– for instance, a narrator may mention a vessel sealer while a bipolar forceps is simultaneously visible but left unaddressed. Treating such a segment as a full scene description would introduce label noise rather than grounded supervision. To address this, we identify Semantic Grounding Moments (SGMs): focused intervals in the transcript where the narrator explicitly anchors a semantic cue to the current surgical scene. SGMs serve as reliable anchors for structured QA generation, since they represent moments of intentional visual–linguistic correspondence. Figure 6 illustrates representative SGMs across multiple semantic categories in the transcript of a surgical video.

B.2.3 Multi-Agent Data synthesis details

Model and inference configuration. All generator and validator agents are built on gpt-5-2025-08-28 (OpenAI), with the reasoning parameter set to high to maximize generation quality. Generator agents are queried at temperature T=0.1T{=}0.1 to allow mild variation across repeated runs while preserving factual consistency. Validator agents are queried at temperature T=0.0T{=}0.0 to enforce deterministic, rule-based judgments. Because GPT-5 is a proprietary API model, exact regeneration remains dependent on continued access to this model version and may be affected by provider-side changes.

Specialized agent pairs. We instantiate K=10K{=}10 generator–validator agent pairs (20 agents in total), one per semantic category, each equipped with detailed system prompts specifying its role, generation instructions, and validation constraints. Table 7 summarizes the key instructions and constraints for each agent pair (Full prompts available in the anonymized repository).

Multi-call generation. Each generator agent is invoked R=3R{=}3 times per transcript. Given that a single call can miss opportunities for QA generation within a given transcript, we run three independent calls to increase overall recall on finding SGMs and generating QAs from them. The combined outputs of all RR calls are then passed jointly to the paired validator, which validates each candidate sample and removes semantic near-duplicates.

Validation criteria. Additional to applying the category-specific constraints listed in Table 7, the validator enforces three universal filtering rules on every generated sample:

  • •

    Hallucination filtering. A sample is discarded if the question or correct answer introduces an entity, action, or clinical claim absent from the paired transcript segment.

  • •

    Visual grounding. A sample is discarded if the question and its ground-truth answer correspond to a narration comment that is not referring to the present visual scene (e.g. comments referring to events that took place in the past, generic procedural information, etc).

  • •

    Temporal window correctness. A sample is discarded if its assigned temporal window does not cover the transcript segment from which the correct answer is derived.

  • •

    Semantic deduplication. Near-duplicate samples arising from multiple generator calls are identified and collapsed. Only the most informative candidate is retained.

Structured output schemas. To enable downstream parsing, both agents are prompted to return structured JSON with reasoning traces justifying its decisions. Listing  and Listing  show the generator and validator output schemas, respectively.

Quantitative summary. Stage 1 processes the transcripts of all 3,148 videos in the corpus, of which 2,478 (78.7%) produced at least one validated QA sample (train: 2,211 | val: 267), yielding 198,248 agent-validated samples in total – 176,593 in the training split and 21,655 in the validation split, leading to a total cost of approximately 20,000 USD. Table 6 reports the sample count and relative frequency per semantic category for each split and the full corpus. The per-category proportions are broadly consistent across splits.

B.3 Stage 2: Multi-Model Retrieval-Augmented Distractor Generation

Stage 1 produces transcript-grounded QA pairs with naively generated multiple-choice distractors. Inspection of these distractors reveals two compounding failure modes. First, correct answers and distractors differ in word length, vocabulary, and level of clinical specificity because distractors are generated from the LLM’s base knowledge distribution while the correct answers are derived from the transcript. Overall, this creates surface shortcuts that allow LLMs to identify the correct answer without any visual grounding (see Stage 1 distractors in Figure 7 for representative examples). Second, distractors generated by a LLMs share model-specific syntactic patterns and vocabulary, introducing an additional model-artifact shortcut that is even more harmful during fine-tuning, when the model can learn from these patterns.

Stage 2 mitigates both failure modes through a two-component strategy: Retrieval-Augmented Distractor Generation (RADG) to align the distractor distribution and style with that of correct answers, and multi-model mixing to suppress model-specific artifacts. The following sections detail the implementation of each component.

B.3.1 Retrieval-Augmented Distractor Generation (RADG)

Embedding model and pool construction. All correct answers in the training set are encoded with BAAI/bge-m3 [13], a dense text embedding model optimized for retrieval-augmented generation and semantic similarity search. Each embedding is stored in a vector database alongside four metadata fields: procedure type, specialty, subject, and question type.

Per-question retrieval. For each question Qi​jkQ_{ij}^{k} we query four metadata-filtered pools, retrieving the top 100 candidates per pool ranked by cosine similarity to the query embedding: answers matching the same procedure type, specialty, and subject as the source video, plus a broad pool spanning all answers of the same question type with no further metadata restriction. This yields a total of 400 exemplar candidates of correct answers in the dataset across pools.

Merging and deduplication. Candidates from the four pools are merged into the exemplar set Ei​jkE_{ij}^{k} by iterating through them in priority order (procedure →\to specialty →\to subject →\to broad). Candidates already present in the merged list are discarded, yielding a deduplicated exemplar set of at most K=100K{=}100 answers that is then passed to distractor generators as answer-style references for the present question.

Distractor Generators. We instantiate three distractor-generator LLMs available on Hugging Face under the following identifiers:

  • •

    M1M_{1}: google/medgemma-27b-text-it [51]

  • •

    M2M_{2}: meta-llama/Llama-3.1-70B [25]

  • •

    M3M_{3}: Qwen/Qwen3.5-35B-A3B [57]

Each generator produces N=6N{=}6 distractors per question, yielding a combined pool of 3​N=183N{=}18 candidates.

Generation conditioning. Each generator MℓM_{\ell} is conditioned on the question Qi​jkQ_{ij}^{k}, its correct answer Ai​jkA_{ij}^{k}, the original option set 𝒪i​jk\mathcal{O}_{ij}^{k}, the local transcript context window Hi​jkH_{ij}^{k}, the retrieved exemplar set Ei​jkE_{ij}^{k}, and video-level metadata mim_{i}:

𝒪i​jk,ℓ=Mℓ​(Qi​jk,Ai​jk,𝒪i​jk,Hi​jk,Ei​jk,mi).\mathcal{O}_{ij}^{k,\ell}=M_{\ell}\!\left(Q_{ij}^{k},\;A_{ij}^{k},\;\mathcal{O}_{ij}^{k},\;H_{ij}^{k},\;E_{ij}^{k},\;m_{i}\right). (4)

Implementation details. All distractor generators are served via vLLM [27] on 4×\times NVIDIA H200 GPUs with T=0.1T{=}0.1. Requests are dispatched asynchronously with a concurrency limit of 128 (35B and 27B models) or 64 (122B models) in-flight calls. End-to-end distractor generation for the entire dataset takes approximately 6.4 days: Qwen3.5-35B (4.5 d), LLaMA-70B (1.2 d), and MedGemma-27B (0.7 d).

The same system prompt is applied identically to all three generators and is shown in Figure 8. We instruct generators to produce distractors whose length, vocabulary, and specificity are indistinguishable from the correct-answer style of the provided exemplar, while still being grounded on the transcript context.

Multi-model mixing. Each of the three generators contributes N=6N{=}6 distractors to the combined pool 𝒟i​jk,pool=𝒪i​jk,M1∪𝒪i​jk,M2∪𝒪i​jk,M3\mathcal{D}_{ij}^{k,\mathrm{pool}}=\mathcal{O}_{ij}^{k,M_{1}}\cup\mathcal{O}_{ij}^{k,M_{2}}\cup\mathcal{O}_{ij}^{k,M_{3}}. The final distractor set is drawn by random sampling from this pool subject to a cross-model diversity constraint, ensuring that the selected distractors are not all sourced from a single generator.

Blind validation. We validate each distractor setup by measuring whether models can exploit linguistic artifacts under blind testing: the model receives only the question and answer options, with no video input, and must select the correct answer. Effective distractor refinement should drive blind-tested accuracy toward the random-choice baseline (prand=0.250p_{\mathrm{rand}}=0.250 for 3 distractors and 0.1430.143 for 6 distractors).

We evaluate two conditions. The off-the-shelf (OS) condition applies the model directly under blind testing without any task-specific training, measuring whether the distractor configuration is exploitable at inference time. To assess for shortcut patterns that a zero-shot model cannot exploit but may become learnable once the model is exposed to the distractor distribution during training, the blind fine-tuning (FT) condition trains the same model exclusively on (question, options) pairs – no video – for the distractor variant being evaluated, then evaluates it under blind testing.

Model and training configuration. Both OS and FT conditions use the Qwen/Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct [8] multimodal model. Blind fine-tuning is performed for one epoch with full LLM fine-tuning (no layers frozen), using a learning rate of 1×10−51\times 10^{-5}, a per-device batch size of 12, and 4 NVIDIA H200 GPUs.

Quantitative Results. Table 8 reports blind-tested accuracy for all configurations under both conditions and both distractor counts (3 and 6). RADG alone reduces OS blind accuracy across all three generators relative to their unaugmented counterparts, confirming that exemplar-conditioned generation narrows the distributional gap. Multi-model mixing further reduces OS accuracy in both settings, with LLM-Mix achieving the lowest blind accuracy overall (0.4010.401 for 3 distractors; 0.2770.277 for 6 distractors). The FT results reveal that the resampled baseline achieves competitive FT scores despite higher OS scores: resampled distractors are harder for fine-tuned models to exploit but remain vulnerable at zero-shot inference time. LLM-Mix reduces OS blind accuracy most consistently across both distractor counts and both evaluation conditions, making it the preferred configuration for the final benchmark. Importantly, RADG reduces blind accuracy across all three model families, while their mixture performs best overall, suggesting that the refinement strategy is not dependent on a single distractor generator.

Qualitative results. While semantic differences between naive distractors and correct answers–such as clinical specificity or depth of medical knowledge–are difficult to quantify directly, one surface-level characteristic stands out clearly: response length. Correct answers tend to be more explicit and precise, making them longer than naive distractors. This length asymmetry is a spurious cue that off-the-shelf models can exploit to identify the correct answer without any task-specific fine-tuning. Figure 9 quantifies this gap by plotting the word-count distributions of correct answers, baseline distractors, and LLM-Mix distractors across all multiple-choice samples in the training set. Baseline distractors exhibit shorter sentences compared to correct answers. In contrast, LLM-Mix distractors–conditioned on retrieved exemplars via RADG–closely match the correct-answer distribution in terms of length.

B.4 Stage 3: Visual-Dependence Curation Details

As reported in Table 8, blind fine-tuning on the refined distractor set drives accuracy above 70%70\% without any video input, confirming that residual language shortcuts persist even after Stage 2 refinement. Stage 3 removes samples solvable without visual evidence by applying a blind-testing consistency filter to both the training set (via cross-validation) and the validation set.

B.4.1 Training Set Cross-Validation Setup

The 2,211 training videos that produced at least one validated QA sample are partitioned into four folds via stratified splitting on procedure subject, ensuring that the subject distribution is balanced across folds. Figure 10 shows the resulting subject distribution per fold, Table 9 summarizes the video and QA counts per fold, and Table 10 reports the per-category QA breakdown.

B.4.2 Guesser Ensemble and Curation Protocol

Guesser composition. The ensemble 𝒢\mathcal{G} comprises four guesser types, all evaluated under blind testing: (i) models blind-fine-tuned on the refined distractors 𝒟ref\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{ref}}; (ii) models blind-fine-tuned on the baseline (Stage 1) distractors; (iii) an off-the-shelf base model with no fine-tuning; and (iv) models fine-tuned with full video access but evaluated under blind testing, which expose shortcuts that video-trained models may absorb from language co-occurrences during training. Types (i)–(iii) are used for training-set curation; the full ensemble (i)–(iv) is used for validation-set curation.

Model and inference configuration. All guessers instantiate Qwen/Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct [8], the same architecture used in Stage 2 (Sec. B.3). Ensemble diversity therefore arises from the training setup: the same model is used off-the-shelf and in fine-tuned variants to find language shortcuts (on refined distractors, on baseline distractors, and with full video access), and all guessers are queried in text-only mode.

Blind fine-tuned guessers (types (i)–(ii), and (iv) for validation-set curation) are trained for one epoch with a learning rate of 1×10−51\times 10^{-5} on 4 NVIDIA H200 GPUs. Temporal Ordering; Sequence Summarization is excluded, as summarizing would require the video and no distractors are used.

Consistency score and thresholds. Each guesser g∈𝒢g\in\mathcal{G} is queried R=5R{=}5 times at temperature T=0.7T{=}0.7 with no video input, receiving only the question Qi​jkQ_{ij}^{k} and the refined options 𝒪i​jk,ref\mathcal{O}_{ij}^{k,\mathrm{ref}}. Repeated queries are necessary because a single blind query carries a non-negligible probability of a correct random guess, which would cause spurious removal of visually grounded samples. The consistency score is the fraction of runs in which gg recovers the correct answer:

S(g,xi​jk)=1R∑r=1R[gr(Qi​jk,𝒪i​jk,ref)=Ai​jk],S(g,x_{ij}^{k})=\frac{1}{R}\sum_{r=1}^{R}\mathbf{1}\!\left[g_{r}\!\left(Q_{ij}^{k},\;\mathcal{O}_{ij}^{k,\mathrm{ref}}\right)=A_{ij}^{k}\right], (5)

so that filtering targets only samples reliably solvable from text alone rather than those guessed correctly by chance. A sample is retained only if no guesser reaches the consistency threshold τ=3/5\tau{=}3/5:

xi​jkretained⟺maxg∈𝒢S(g,xi​jk)<τ,x_{ij}^{k}\ \text{retained}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\max_{g\in\mathcal{G}}\,S(g,x_{ij}^{k})<\tau, (6)

i.e. a sample is discarded whenever any guesser achieves S≥3/5S\geq 3/5.

Training set curation. For each fold ff, guessers of types (i)–(iii) are trained on the three complementary folds and scored on the held-out fold.

Validation set curation. All guesser types (i)–(iv) are trained on the full Sureon training set and evaluated on the validation set.

Sureon-DB quality proxy. We use the out-of-fold blind-test pass rate as a proxy for text-answerable contamination in the automatically generated training data. Of the 161,667 training samples eligible for blind curation (all types except Sequence Summarization), 61,135 (37.8%) pass the criterion above, while 100,532 (62.2%) are identified as consistently answerable from text alone and removed. By construction, every sample retained in Sureon-DB passes the held-out blind-guesser criterion, providing a sample-level quality control against language shortcuts without requiring expert review of the full training corpus.

B.4.3 Distractor Hardening via Iterative Blind Testing

As a final curation step applied to the validation set, we fine-tune Qwen/Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct [8] on the full curated training set Sureon-DB using text only (question and answer options, no video) for 1010 epochs with a learning rate of 1×10−51\times 10^{-5} on 4 NVIDIA H200 GPUs. Training for longer than in Sec. B.4.2 produces a stronger adversary that has more thoroughly absorbed any residual shortcut patterns in the training distribution.

For each retained validation sample, we search for the distractor configuration from the pool 𝒟i​jk,pool\mathcal{D}_{ij}^{k,\mathrm{pool}} generated in Stage 2 that the hardened guesser fails to answer correctly under blind testing. Up to M=32M{=}32 candidate distractor configurations are drawn at random (seed=42) from 𝒟i​jk,pool\mathcal{D}_{ij}^{k,\mathrm{pool}}; the first configuration for which the guesser fails (S<τ=3/5S<\tau{=}3/5) is retained as the final distractor set. If no such configuration is found within the MM attempts, the sample is discarded. Algorithm 1 formalizes this procedure.

Held-out guesser generalization. To test whether hardening overfits to the model family used during curation, we additionally evaluate Gemma-4-31B-IT, which is not used at any stage of blind filtering or distractor hardening, under the same text-only condition. For the Qwen3 model trained on SUREON, blind accuracy decreases from 36.5% on the pre-hardening validation set to 21.4% after hardening. Gemma-4-31B-IT remains comparably low across the same sets (23.2% to 22.9%). Thus, while hardening primarily removes shortcuts learned by the adversary used during curation, the resulting samples remain difficult for a held-out model family, providing evidence that the procedure does not simply specialize the benchmark against Qwen-specific failure modes.

Table 11 reports per-category sample counts at each stage of curation: training and validation after blind-testing filtering (Sec. B.4.2), and the validation set after distractor hardening. Sequence Summarization is excluded from curation and hardening; all SM samples are carried through unchanged from Stage 1.

Training set curation ablation. To validate that curating the training set encourages models to ground predictions in visual evidence, we compare two training configurations: a model trained on the full uncurated set 𝒟ref\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{ref}} and a model trained on the curated set Sureon-DB, both evaluated on the hardened validation set. Training on the curated set is expected to yield higher vision-enabled accuracy, as the model is no longer rewarded for exploiting language shortcuts during training. Figure 11 reports vision and blind accuracy under both training conditions.

B.5 Stage 4: Expert Verification Details

The hardened validation set 𝒟val⋆\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{val}}^{\star} produced by Stage 3 is submitted to manual verification by expert surgeons; no additional LLM-based filtering or adjudication is applied at this stage. Only samples that pass expert review are retained in the final Sureon benchmark ℬSureon\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{\textsc{Sureon}}}.

B.5.1 Annotation Platform

Verification is conducted on a dedicated web-based annotation platform. Figure 12 shows the main verification screen, which presents: (i) the video clip and its timestamp, (ii) the question with all answer options (the correct answer marked in green), and (iii) an approve/reject interface requiring a written note for every rejection. Figure 13 shows the extended context view, available by scrolling below the verification screen, which provides the full surgery video (starting at the clip’s timestamp), the aligned transcript segment, and video-level metadata including title, specialty, procedure, and QA type. Reviewers are encouraged to consult the full video whenever the short clip is insufficient to make a judgement. The platform also exposes specialty, procedure, and QA type filters, allowing reviewers to focus on samples within their clinical domain.

B.5.2 Reviewer Panel and Protocol

Verification is conducted by 6 surgeons affiliated to different institutions.

Sample assignment. Each sample is assigned to a single reviewer, drawn uniformly at random from the pool of available samples across the different question types, and reviewers may skip any sample they consider outside their domain. A single reviewer per sample is sufficient because reviewers do not annotate from scratch: each candidate QA is already transcript-grounded, with its correct answer derived from a surgeon’s narration (Sec. B.2). Verification is therefore a confirmation step rather than an open-ended labeling task, in which the reviewer checks video–transcript alignment, the clinical correctness of the narration-derived answer, and distractor validity for the specific clip. Because the underlying supervision already originates from a domain expert, a single qualified reviewer suffices to confirm these conditions, and we apply a conservative retention policy under which any rejected or flagged sample is discarded, so that residual subjectivity removes samples rather than admitting incorrect ones.

Inter-rater reliability. Although each benchmark candidate was reviewed by one surgeon in the primary verification protocol, we independently dual-reviewed a subset of 74 QA samples distributed among QA types to estimate inter-rater agreement. Each sample was independently reviewed by two raters drawn from a pool of five surgeons, with reviewer pairs assigned to ensure balanced coverage across all C(5,2)=10 possible pairings. The two reviewers independently rendered the same binary approve/reject decision and agreed on 52 of 74 samples (70.3% agreement). The duplicate ratings were used only to estimate agreement and did not alter the primary single-review retention decision.

Review criteria. Each reviewer watches the clip and assesses the following four conditions, all of which must hold simultaneously for a sample to be approved:

  • •

    Question soundness. The question is clear, clinically meaningful, and answerable from the specific clip or segment provided.

  • •

    Answer correctness. The marked answer is clinically correct and is visible or directly supported within the clip’s time window.

  • •

    Video–transcript alignment. The QA reflects what is actually shown in the clip, and the clip depicts a real operative scene rather than, e.g., a slide or diagram.

  • •

    Distractor validity. All distractors are clinically plausible for the context but unambiguously incorrect for this specific clip. Any sample for which a second option could also be correct is rejected.

Reviewers are additionally asked to confirm that the question requires the video to answer and cannot be resolved from generic procedural knowledge alone, serving as a human analog of the blind-testing filter applied in Stage 3. We encourage rejected samples to include a brief written note identifying the reason for rejection.

For Forecasting questions, the correct answer describes the step that occurs after the clip ends and therefore cannot be verified from the clip alone. Reviewers are instructed to note the clip’s end timestamp, open the full video, and confirm that the marked next step actually occurs immediately after the clip before approving.

Quantitative summary. Table 12 reports the number of reviewed, approved, and rejected samples per category, along with the approval rate. The experts provided rejection reasons for 178 and the breakdown is distributed as follows: 22.5% flagged as ambiguous/multiple-correct, 14.6% inaccurate, 9.6% too-short or insufficient context, and 9.6% not visible in the video. The final benchmark ℬSureon\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{\textsc{Sureon}}} comprises all approved samples across categories. Expert verification required approximately 32 hours of cumulative surgeon time across all reviewers.

B.6 Final Dataset Configuration

We consolidate the configuration retained after all four stages; per-stage counts are in Tab. 11 and key attributes in Tab. 2. The pipeline yields two resources from a common process. Sureon-DB is the curated training database: of the 2,211 training videos with validated Stage-1 QA, 2,191 retain at least one sample after blind-testing curation (Sec. B.4), giving 76,06176{,}061 QA pairs. The Sureon benchmark is the expert-verified set: the hardened validation set 𝒟val⋆\mathcal{D}^{\star}_{\mathrm{val}} is reviewed by surgeons (Sec. B.5), and the 340340 approved samples, from 165165 distinct source videos, form ℬSureon\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{\textsc{Sureon}}}. The two splits share no source videos, as splitting is video-level prior to generation (Sec. B). Figure 14 shows the hierarchical distribution of both resources across surgical specialties and subjects.

Distractor configuration. Each multiple-choice question is paired with six distractors via LLM-Mix: the three generators (M1M_{1}, M2M_{2}, M3M_{3}) each emit six candidates, and the final six are drawn from the 1818-candidate pool. We adopt this six-distractor LLM-Mix setting because it most consistently drives blind-tested accuracy toward chance across both off-the-shelf and fine-tuned conditions (Tab. 8). In Sureon-DB these are the curated Stage-2 sets; in the benchmark they are the configurations selected by iterative hardening (Sec. B.4.3). Sequence Summarization is open-ended and carries no distractors.

Appendix C Training Data Construction from public dataset sources

In the main paper (Sec. 3.2) we consolidate Sureon with supervision derived from existing public surgical datasets to study two questions: whether the standard perception-centric training recipe transfers to reasoning (Q1), and whether combining both sources yields a single model that is strong at perception and reasoning (Q2). This appendix details how we transform that public data — denoted 𝒟pub\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{pub}} in the main text — into instruction-tuning QA pairs that share Sureon’s format. We deliberately follow a similar recipe used by prior surgical assistants [9, 76]: (1) unification of heterogeneous annotations into a common schema, (2) rendering of those annotations into natural-language QA pairs via task-specific templates, and (3) LLM-based linguistic augmentation. After stage 1 the pipeline diverges into an image branch (frame-level perception tasks) and a clip branch (workflow/temporal-segmentation tasks). Combined with Sureon-DB, the result is the consolidated corpus 𝒟all=𝒟Sureon-DB∪𝒟pub\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{all}}=\mathcal{D}_{\text{{Sureon}-DB}}\cup\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{pub}}..

C.1 Stage 1: Common Annotation Schema

Each public dataset ships with its own annotation format, label vocabulary, and temporal representation. We normalize all datasets into a single relational schema that captures: dataset-level capability flags (has_phase, has_tool_bbox, has_triplets, etc.); video metadata (split, frame rate, total frames); per-frame classification labels (phase, step, action indices, tool/anatomy presence lists); per-frame object instances (class, bounding box in, optional segmentation mask stored as a COCO RLE); temporal segments (start/end frame, segment type); and inter-object relations (instrument–verb–target triplets).

Canonical vocabulary. Dataset-specific label names are normalized to a shared canonical vocabulary. For the image branch this mapping is stored in a flat reverse-lookup dictionary covering tools, anatomical structures, surgical phases, procedural steps, and action verbs (e.g., CalotTriangleDissection to calot triangle dissection; hook to electrocautery hook). For the clip branch an equivalent per-dataset mapping handles the same normalization, and each dataset is further annotated with its procedure type.

Source datasets. The image branch covers 17 source datasets (CholecT50 [41], CholecInstanceSeg [1], CholecSeg8k [26], GraSP [5], EndoVis2017 [2], EndoVis2018 [3], Endoscapes [39], AutoLaparo [64], LapGyn [30], Phakir [45], HeiChole [59], HeiCo [36], GynSurg [40], Dresden [11], HemoSet [37]), providing tool presence and localization, anatomy localization, instrument–verb–target triplets, Critical View of Safety (CVS), and frame-level phase/action labels. The clip branch covers 13 source datasets (Cholec80 [58], AutoLaparo, GraSP, GynSurg, HeiChole, HeiCo-Proctocolectomy, HeiCo-Rectal Resection, HeiCo-Sigmoid Resection, MultiBypass [29], Phakir, SARRARP50 [43], SurgicalActions160 [48]), providing continuous temporal annotations for phases, steps, actions, and tool presence. Eight datasets contribute to both branches, for 22 distinct sources in total; Table 13 lists each dataset, the branches it feeds, and the resulting sample counts.

C.2 Stage 2a: Image-Level QA Template Generation

Segmentation-to-instance conversion. Several datasets provide only semantic segmentation masks. For each class we apply a conversion policy: single-instance classes (anatomical structures known to appear once, such as the gallbladder or uterus) are treated as a single pseudo-instance by taking the union of all connected components, then fitting a tight bounding box; connected-components classes (blood pools, clips) are split into individual pseudo-instances via 8-connected-component labeling, sorted top-to-bottom then left-to-right by centroid; and strict-semantic classes (large background structures such as the abdominal wall or liver bed) are retained as presence-only annotations without bounding-box assignment. All bounding boxes are normalized to a [0,1000][0,1000] coordinate space and stored in [x1,y1,x2,y2][x_{1},y_{1},x_{2},y_{2}] format.

QA types. Starting from the normalized frame annotations, we instantiate task-specific QA templates across two families. Open-ended templates produce free-text answers and cover: tool/anatomy presence (“Which surgical instruments are visible?”); counting (“How many surgical instruments are visible?”); view-region localization (“Where is the {tool} with respect to the surgical field?”); action presence (“What action is happening in this frame?”; triplet recognition (“What is the {tool} doing?”); Critical View of Safety (three binary criteria for safe cholecystectomy); mask classification (identify structures from rendered contour overlays); and procedure-type recognition. Binary and negative variants are generated by sampling negative class labels from the dataset vocabulary.

Grounded templates. Grounded templates instead require structured JSON answers, which lets us pose localization and recognition tasks with machine-checkable outputs. They span localization (returning a JSON array of labeled, indexed bounding boxes for the visible tools or anatomy), presence (a dictionary flagging each class as present or absent), counting (the number of tools in view), phase and step recognition (the active phase or step), triplet recognition (the active instrument–verb–target relations), and action recognition (the action performed by each tool in view). In every grounded template the question explicitly enumerates the full class vocabulary as the option set, anchoring the model to a closed label space. Each QA pair is serialized as a JSONL record with the question, answer, an optional reasoning trace (omitted for non-CoT types), and provenance fields identifying the QA type, source dataset, file, video, and frame.

C.3 Stage 2b: Video Clip QA Template Generation

Clip sampling. For temporal datasets we sample variable-length clips with two strategies. By default, strategic sampling biases selection toward phase and step transition boundaries and stable mid-phase regions, so that clips capture both the moments of change and the steady states between them. Alternatively, grounded clip sampling slides a fixed 8-frame window with a stride of four and keeps a clip only if it lies entirely within a single constant-label segment across all requested tasks (phase, step, action), guaranteeing an unambiguous answer.

Language templates. For each sampled clip, a clip-description generator draws at random from several templates and fills them with the clip’s annotations. Phase and step templates describe which phase or step the clip shows, and optionally enrich this with the procedure type, the temporal position within the phase (beginning, middle, or end), or both; clips that span a boundary instead use transition templates that name the two phases and the approximate time of the switch, the procedure transitions from {phase1} to {phase2}”). Step templates extend this to single-, two-, and multi-step sequences, action templates to the actions present, and tool templates to which instruments appear and when they are used (e.g., “{tool} is used from {start} s to {end} s”).

Question types. The resulting questions are descriptive (“What is happening in this clip?”), binary (“Is the {phase} phase shown in this clip?”), temporal (“When does {event} occur in this clip?”), or counting (“How many distinct phases are shown?”). As in the image branch, grounded clip questions take a structured JSON answer (e.g., the active phase). For each dataset we keep three versions of every QA pair — the direct template output, an instruction-style rephrasing, and an LLM-augmented variant (Sec. C.4) — which are pooled at training time.

C.4 Stage 3: LLM-Based Linguistic Augmentation

To increase linguistic diversity without altering factual content, we paraphrase each templated QA pair with an Qwen3.5-9B [57], adding one rephrased variant per pair to the training pool.

Image branch. We use Qwen3.5-9B [57] (T=0.7T{=}0.7, p=0.8p{=}0.8, k=20k{=}20, up to 256 new tokens) to rephrase the question and answer under three constraints: surgical terminology is preserved exactly (phase, step, procedure, and action are never interchanged), the question retains explicit visual-grounding cues (e.g., “in this image”, “visible in the frame”), and any ordered or list structure in the original is kept intact. For tasks with structured answers (localization, presence, triplet, and mask classification), only the question is paraphrased and the answer is copied verbatim, so it remains valid and label-consistent. For chain-of-thought samples, the accompanying reasoning is paraphrased alongside the question and answer.

Clip branch. We use Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct [8] in text-only mode (T=0.7T{=}0.7, p=0.9p{=}0.9, up to 256 new tokens) with an analogous prompt that additionally requires each question to refer to a video clip or segment and, as above, keeps phase, step, and action distinct.

Appendix D Evaluation

This section specifies the inference and scoring protocols used in our experiments (Sec. 4), covering the Sureon benchmark (Tab. 3) and the public perception benchmarks for recognition and spatial grounding (Tab. 5, Tab. 19). All close-ended questions and Temporal Ordering are evaluated under accuracy. The open-ended Sequence Summarization (SM) type is scored by an LLM judge (Claude Opus 4.8) using the prompt in Fig. 15. We organize the protocols into evaluation on Sureon (Sec. D.1) and on public benchmarks (Sec. D.3).

D.1 SUREON Benchmark Evaluation

Frame sampling and inference. Every model receives the same visual input for a given question. For each clip we uniformly sample up to 8 frames across its duration at the video’s frame rate, clamped to a minimum of 4 frames. Before inference, we apply a two-stage blurring pass to the sampled frames: a YOLO-based non-surgical object detector identifies non-operative regions (faces, equipment logos, and other non-surgical content) trained for YouTube videos [12], and optical character recognition detects on-screen textual overlays such as procedure labels, instrument names in the user interface, and equipment text; both sets of detected regions are blurred. Surgical academic videos can contain these overlays, which modern VLMs may exploit through OCR to infer answers without interpreting the underlying surgical scene; blurring them prevents this source of leakage and better isolates visual surgical understanding. Each frame in the prompt is tagged with its absolute timestamp, preceded by the clip’s time range, followed by the question and the option list (prompt template in Fig. 17). The question text, option set, and option order are held fixed across all evaluated models.

Option format. Multiple-choice questions are presented with seven options giving a random baseline of 1/7=14.3%1/7=14.3\%. Temporal Ordering (TO) requires ordering three events, for which the random baseline over the 3!=63!=6 permutations is 1/6=16.7%1/6=16.7\%. Distractor selection and option shuffling are seeded per sample for reproducibility.

Blind condition and multimodal gain. The blind condition removes the visual input entirely: the model receives a text-only payload containing the identical question and option list, with no frames. We report multimodal gain MG=Sv−Sw​v\mathrm{MG}=S_{v}-S_{wv} as the accuracy difference between the visual (SvS_{v}) and blind (Sw​vS_{wv}) passes.

Scoring. The eight multiple-choice types are scored by exact-match accuracy against the correct option. For TO, we extract the predicted sequence of event labels from the free-form output and require exact, order-sensitive equality with the reference sequence. SM is scored by the LLM judge described below. Reported μ\mu is the pooled accuracy over the 299 accuracy-scored items; SM is reported separately and excluded from μ\mu.

Human baseline protocol. The human baseline is collected from 5 surgeons, a subset of the 6-surgeon panel used for Stage 4 expert verification; Sequence Summarization is excluded from the baseline due to the time cost of open-ended grading, leaving 299 accuracy-scored items. Baseline collection uses a separate interface from the verification platform: each surgeon is shown only the video clip, the question, and the answer options (no blind testing mode for expert baseline). Items are distributed uniformly at random across QA types for each surgeon, without matching raters to their own specialty, as our reviewer pool is not large enough to guarantee specialty coverage per item. Each item is answered by a single surgeon, and the reported score aggregates across raters. To avoid trivial recall, no surgeon is shown a question they had already adjudicated during expert verification. After each answer, surgeons self-report confidence (Confident / Somewhat / Not confident); across recorded responses the breakdown is 31.4% / 37.5% / 17.7%, with 13.4% not recorded. Total collection required approximately 8.5 hours of cumulative surgeon time. Several surgeons reported difficulty answering questions outside their own specialty, consistent with the per-category gap between near-ceiling performance on Procedure-Agnostic Action Description and comparatively weaker performance on categories that require specialty-specific understanding, which also motivates a surgical VLM capable of breadth across specialties, which no single human specialist reviewer possesses.

Uncertainty and statistical comparisons. We quantify uncertainty in the Sureon results using 95% confidence intervals. For the overall accuracy, we verify our non-parametric bootstrap intervals (10,000 resamples over benchmark items) against the analytic Wilson score interval. The two estimates closely agree, with a mean absolute discrepancy of 0.25 percentage points and a maximum of 0.54 points across all model estimates. We additionally bootstrap accuracy separately for each question category and for the perception and reasoning aggregates, and we report a surgeon baseline collected under the same video-based protocol as the model evaluations. Because model (and surgeon) predictions are paired on the same benchmark samples, pairwise differences are tested using McNemar’s test with Holm–Bonferroni correction across all (122)=66\binom{12}{2}=66 model pairs (11 evaluated models and the human baseline). Tables 14, 15, 16, and 17 report the corresponding confidence intervals; Table 18 reports the full pairwise significance matrix underlying the claims above.

Category-level estimates are necessarily less precise because each accuracy-based category contains only 29–37 samples, compared with 299 samples for overall μ\mu. Across the 12 models, the average bootstrap 95% CI half-width is 14.3 percentage points, compared with approximately 5.0 percentage points overall. We therefore use category-level results primarily to characterize task-specific strengths and weaknesses rather than to establish fine-grained model rankings. Perception (n=166n=166) and reasoning (n=133n=133) aggregates provide intermediate precision. Notably, the surgeon baseline attains near-ceiling accuracy on PAD (96.5%) but is markedly lower on EE (51.3%, statistically indistinguishable from several models), suggesting category difficulty is not uniform even for expert humans.

LLM-judge for Sequence Summarization. The SM judge scores each prediction against a fixed transcript-derived reference, not the judge’s own surgical knowledge. Seeing only the two texts, it is prompted to be strict (Fig. 15): a prediction is incorrect if any reference step is missing, if meaningful ordering is violated, or if an action is substituted (e.g. a structure the reference preserves is reported as divided), while paraphrases and surgical synonyms count as matching.

LLM Judge Validation. To validate the judge, three annotators independently rated 44 stratified predictions sampled across all 11 models (4 per model, balanced by verdict). Raters were shown only the question, reference, and extracted prediction and applied the same two-criterion rubric. Inter-rater agreement was moderate (mean pairwise raw agreement 64.5%), consistent with the subjectivity of surgical sequence evaluation. Majority-vote human verdicts agreed with the LLM judge on 79.1% of samples. Disagreements were asymmetric: in 6 of the 10 discordant cases the judge marked a prediction incorrect that humans accepted, versus 3 in the opposite direction, indicating that the judge applies the rubric more strictly than human raters.

D.2 Qualitative Error Analysis

Figure 16 presents representative Sureon-VLM failures across four perception and four reasoning categories, revealing two distinct error modes.

Perception errors are near-misses, not random guesses. Predictions consistently land in the correct local neighborhood of the ground truth rather than on implausible alternatives. In Action Description, the model correctly locates clip application in Calot’s triangle but confuses the cystic artery for the cystic duct. In Entity Existence, “Toldt space” is predicted for “retroperitoneal space,” an adjacent landmark. These suggest coarse scene understanding without the fine-grained discrimination the benchmark targets. The Instrument-Action example is a sharper failure: the model predicts the suction irrigator’s canonical function (clearing blood) over its atypical use in this clip (blunt dissection), which is a language prior-driven error rather than a visual one, and a reminder that dataset-level shortcut removal (RADG, blind-testing) still has limitations in preventing a trained model from defaulting to real-world instrument priors when visual attention is weak.

Reasoning errors tend toward generic, plausible-sounding answers. In Safety Practice Identification, the model describes a real but different aspect of the scene (a dissection step) rather than the specific hemostatic action asked about. Local Action Reasoning shows this most clearly: “maintain orientation within the surgical field” is a generic justification that could apply to nearly any dissection, where the ground truth requires reasoning about a specific plane and proximity to skin. These are fluent, surgically literate answers that fail on specificity. Forecasting errors are comparatively softer, correctly anticipating the coarse next phase while erring on technical detail.

D.3 Public Perception Benchmark Evaluation

Inputs and clip construction. Public benchmarks are evaluated with three input modes depending on the task. Frame-level tasks (tool localization and frame-level phase/action recognition) use a single frame. Clip-level recognition uses a fixed window of 88 frames at a stride of 44 (spanning up to ∼\sim2828 s at 11 fps extraction) anchored on the keyframe. We evaluate all clip tasks in the online setting, where the keyframe is the final frame of the window with preceding frames providing causal context. Sureon-VLM is evaluated in both frame and clip variants where applicable. Commercial and open-source baselines are evaluated in frame-only mode on public benchmarks—commercial models due to inference costs and surgical models due to unavailable weights—using numbers reported in their original papers.

Recognition and classification metrics. Phase and action recognition are scored by video-averaged macro-F1 (per-video macro-F1 averaged over videos), which avoids long videos dominating the aggregate. For Cholec80 we additionally report accuracy, recall, and precision, all video-averaged. For Endoscapes Critical View of Safety (CVS), each of the three criteria (C1–C3) is posed as an independent binary (Yes/No) query (prompts in Fig. 18). We report per-criterion accuracy and the macro-average over C1–C3.

Localization metrics. Tool localization is scored by mAP50, the COCO bounding-box average precision at an IoU threshold of 0.500.50. Because generative models emit boxes without confidence scores, all predicted boxes are assigned a constant score, so every prediction participates in the precision–recall computation. The category universe is defined by the ground-truth class names; predicted labels are canonicalized (lowercased, normalized for spacing and trivial pluralization) before matching.

Test splits and exclusions. Each benchmark is evaluated on its official test split. For Cholec80 clip evaluation we exclude 1717 videos that overlap with training sources from Endoscapes and CholecT50 to prevent train/test leakage 11 1 As suggested in https://github.com/CAMMA-public/camma_dataset_overlaps.

Downstream task prompts. The prompts used to query models for phase recognition, tool localization, and CVS assessment are shown in Fig. 18. Each prompt enumerates the closed label set as the option list and specifies a structured (JSON) answer format to enable checkable scoring.

Appendix E Sureon-VLM training details

A common approach to domain adaptation is vanilla supervised fine-tuning (SFT), which we take as a representative baseline to study how data composition and staging order affect both reasoning and grounding on the Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct backbone. Our adaptation combines two complementary resources: public datasets supplying annotated images and clips for spatial grounding and workflow recognition, and Sureon-DB supplying narration-derived VQA for reasoning over actions, states, and procedural progression. We evaluate on Sureon for visual reasoning alongside four public grounding benchmarks: CholecInstanceSeg and GraSP for tool localization, Cholec80 for phase recognition, and SARRARP-50 for action recognition.

Setup. We vary the data—P (public images), S (Sureon-DB), P + S (full corpus)—and exposure order. Single trains in one stage; P→\rightarrowmix and S→\rightarrowmix warm-start on public images or Sureon video before a second stage on the full mixture; mix1→{}_{1}\rightarrowmix2 splits the mixture into two stages, image-heavy first, then balanced.

Single-source fine-tuning erodes existing capabilities. We read the zero-shot backbone as a reference for forgetting: when training on source AA drops task BB below the untuned base, training has overwritten capability the base already had. Both single-source runs do this. Public-only training raises grounding but drops Sureon (24.7→\rightarrow14.7); Sureon-only raises Sureon but collapses tool localization on CISeg (9.9→\rightarrow3.3). Action recognition (SP50) falls below the base under both (14.5→\rightarrow8.4 public, →\rightarrow7.4 Sureon), and Sureon also degrades phase recognition on C80 (17.2→\rightarrow6.7). Single-source supervision thus sacrifices abilities the model already possessed rather than specializing it.

Staging order determines what is retained. Exposure order matters in the mixed corpus. Public-then-video (P→\rightarrowmix) recovers Sureon but partly forgets the grounding learned first (CISeg 75.9→\rightarrow67.1; GraSP 60.7→\rightarrow59.9). The reverse is more revealing: adding public data after Sureon video lifts Sureon by over three points (43.1→\rightarrow46.0), yet grounding never recovers (GraSP only 42.9, ∼\sim17 points below schedules that see images early). Grounding installed late is harder to add than reasoning layered onto a perception-first model—an asymmetry favoring early image exposure.

Strong downstream scores do not mean the model understands the scene. The combined schedules look like clear wins on the public benchmarks, but these reward fitting a fixed label set, not seeing the scene; adaptation moves capability around more than it adds understanding. Even the balanced schedules, which avoid the worst forgetting, fall short on Sureon and stay sensitive to training order. The open problem is how to adapt a model so it reasons over the surgical scene without forgetting how to see it—which Sureon, requiring perception to answer, is built to track.

Final Sureon-VLM Configuration. Based on this ablation, Sureon-VLM uses the P+S (mix1→{}_{1}\rightarrowmix2) staging schedule, as it achieves the best average performance across Sureon and downstream perception tasks. This model fine-tunes Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct on the consolidated corpus 𝒟all\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{all}} in two stages: Stage 1 with image-heavy composition, Stage 2 with balanced data mixture, as described above.

Training implementation. All runs fully fine-tune Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct (vision encoder, MLP projector, and LLM) for 10 epochs in bfloat16, using AdamW with a learning rate of 2×10−62\times 10^{-6}, a cosine schedule with 10% linear warmup, and no weight decay. We use a per-device batch size of 8 with gradient accumulation of 4 over 6 H200 GPUs (effective batch size 192) under DeepSpeed ZeRO-3, a context length of 8,192 tokens, and 8 frames per clip. For each Sureon-DB multiple-choice item, the distractor set is resampled at random from its Stage-2 candidate pool (Sec. B.3) each time the item is loaded, so option content and ordering vary across epochs as augmentation. Both stages of the best two-stage schedule (mix1→{}_{1}\rightarrowmix2) share these hyperparameters: Stage 1 initializes from the pretrained base with an image-heavy mixture (image 72.7% / clip 14.9% / Sureon-DB 12.4%), and Stage 2 warm-starts from the Stage-1 checkpoint with an equal-thirds mixture to re-balance the sources. Given the relative corpus sizes, the Sureon-DB video data is effectively seen ∼\sim20×\times over the schedule.

Appendix F Ethics

Ethical use of data. Sureon is constructed from publicly available surgical lecture videos and is intended for research use only. Sureon-DB is automatically pseudo-labeled and is not expert-verified; models trained on it are research artifacts and must not be used for clinical decision-making or surgical practice in their current form. The expert-verified benchmark is intended for evaluation, not as clinical ground truth.

Data licensing and usage. Sureon is derived from SurgLaVi-β\beta [42], which is released under the Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-ShareAlike 4.0 International License (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0). In accordance with the ShareAlike provision, we release both Sureon-DB and the Sureon benchmark under the same CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 license, restricting use to non-commercial research and requiring attribution and identical redistribution terms. We release the derived QA annotations, temporal windows, and metadata; the underlying lecture videos remain governed by their original sources and are not redistributed.

De-identification. The source material consists of publicly available educational lecture videos that are edited and narrated for pedagogical purposes; they do not contain patient names, medical record numbers, or other protected health identifiers. Laparoscopic and robot-assisted footage depicts internal anatomy rather than external patient features, inherently limiting re-identification risk.
